title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions Cheat Sheet

introduction.heading: CI/CD: Automating Tests, Builds & Deploys
introduction.description: A practical reference for wiring up a GitHub Actions pipeline that lints and tests every push automatically (Continuous Integration) and deploys automatically once those checks pass (Continuous Deployment) - no separate CI service and no manual npm run deploy required.

prerequisites: A project already pushed to a GitHub repository
package.json scripts for lint/test/build (npm run lint, npm test, npm run build)
Basic YAML familiarity - indentation is meaningful

steps.title: Create the Workflow File & Folder Structure
steps.description: GitHub Actions looks for workflow files in one specific folder at the root of the repo. Any .yml or .yaml file there is picked up automatically - no registration step, no external service to configure.
steps.note: The folder must be named exactly .github/workflows - a typo like .github/workflow (singular) means GitHub silently ignores the file, with no error anywhere.

steps.title: Choose Your Triggers
steps.description: The on: block decides when the workflow runs. push runs it on every push to the listed branches, pull_request runs it for PRs targeting them (so checks show up before a merge), and workflow_dispatch adds a manual "Run workflow" button in the Actions tab.
steps.note: workflow_dispatch takes no inputs here, but you can add them underneath it to pass parameters (e.g. which environment to deploy) when triggering manually.

steps.title: Check Out Code & Set Up Node
steps.description: Every job starts on a brand-new, empty virtual machine, so nothing exists until you put it there. actions/checkout clones the repo; actions/setup-node installs the Node version you ask for and, with cache: "npm", restores npm's cache automatically.
steps.note: Pin node-version to the same major version you develop and deploy with, so a Node-version mismatch never becomes a 'works on my machine' bug.

steps.title: Install, Lint & Test
steps.description: npm ci (not npm install) installs exactly what package-lock.json specifies and fails outright if the lockfile is out of sync with package.json - the deterministic, CI-appropriate counterpart to npm install. Any run: step that exits non-zero fails the whole job and blocks the pull request.
steps.note: Order matters: lint fails fast on style/syntax issues before spending minutes running the full test suite.

steps.title: Matrix Builds Across Node Versions
steps.description: A matrix runs the same job multiple times in parallel, once per value (or combination of values) you list. Here it runs the full install-and-test cycle once per Node version, catching a dependency that only breaks on Node 20 or only on Node 24 before a user ever hits it.
steps.note: Matrices multiply: adding an os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest] axis alongside node-version runs all 3 x 2 = 6 combinations.

steps.title: Cache Dependencies for Faster Runs
steps.description: setup-node's cache: "npm" option from step 3 already covers the common case. This is the underlying mechanism for anything it doesn't: the cache key is derived from the lockfile's hash, so a cache is reused until dependencies actually change and is invalidated automatically the moment they do.
steps.note: Never cache node_modules itself across OS or Node-version boundaries - native binary dependencies (like sharp or bcrypt) won't be compatible with a different platform.

steps.title: Store Secrets & Environment Variables
steps.description: Secrets - API keys, deploy tokens, database URLs - never belong in the YAML file itself. They're masked wherever they'd appear in logs and stored encrypted, and are referenced with ${{ secrets.NAME }}. Non-secret configuration can use ${{ vars.NAME }} (repository variables) instead, which are visible in the UI but not encrypted.
substeps: Name it (e.g. VITE_API_URL), paste the value, and click "Add secret"
steps.note: Secrets aren't available to workflows triggered by a pull_request from a forked repository, by design - it stops a malicious PR from exfiltrating your tokens.

steps.title: Build & Upload Artifacts
steps.description: Uploading the build output as an artifact makes it downloadable from the workflow run's summary page, and is how a later job (or a separate deploy workflow) picks up exactly what CI just built and tested, instead of rebuilding it from scratch.
steps.note: retention-days keeps storage usage (and cost, on private repos) down - artifacts you only need for inspecting a failed run don't need to live for 90 days.

steps.title: Deploy to GitHub Pages on Merge (CD)
steps.description: needs: build-and-test makes this job wait for CI to pass first, and the if: condition restricts it to pushes on main - so a pull request never deploys, only a merge does. This is Continuous Deployment: the last manual step (npm run deploy, run by hand) disappears entirely. This repo's own workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) builds the app and pushes dist/ straight to a gh-pages branch with peaceiris/actions-gh-pages - no Pages-specific permissions or artifact upload/download step required.
substeps: Set Source to "Deploy from a branch", Branch to gh-pages, and the folder to / (root)
steps.note: permissions: contents: write is required on the deploy job - without it, the default GITHUB_TOKEN can't push the gh-pages branch that peaceiris/actions-gh-pages creates, and the job fails with a permissions error even though everything else is correct.

subSteps.title: Optional: Deploy via GitHub's Official Pages Action Instead
subSteps.description: If you'd rather have Pages serve the build directly from an Actions run instead of publishing a gh-pages branch, swap the peaceiris job for actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages. It needs its own permissions (pages: write, id-token: write) and an environment: github-pages block, and requires the repo's Pages source to be set to "GitHub Actions" rather than "Deploy from a branch".
subSteps.note: Both approaches are valid - the gh-pages-branch method above is simpler and is what this repo actually uses; this one avoids keeping a build artifact in git history at the cost of a slightly more involved permissions setup.

steps.title: Add a Status Badge
steps.description: Drop this into your README so the pass/fail state of the latest run on the default branch is visible at a glance, without opening the Actions tab.
steps.note: Replace <owner> and <repo>, and ci.yml with your actual workflow filename if it differs.

steps.title: Common Errors & Fixes
steps.description: The errors you'll hit most often when setting up a pipeline for the first time, and what they actually mean.
steps.note: When a run fails for a reason that isn't obvious, re-run it with "Enable debug logging" from the re-run dropdown before assuming the workflow itself is broken.

gettingStarted.heading: Quick Checklist
steps: Define on: push / pull_request / workflow_dispatch triggers
npm ci, then npm run lint and npm test
Add secrets under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions
Add a deploy job with needs: build-and-test, an if: branch guard, and permissions: contents: write
Build, then push dist/ to gh-pages with peaceiris/actions-gh-pages (or use the optional actions/deploy-pages job instead)
Set the Pages source to the gh-pages branch in repo Settings (or "GitHub Actions" if you used the optional approach)
Add the status badge to your README
